source.title: Learned Random Label Predictions as a Neural Network Complexity Metric

record.tranche_reason: Measures random-label prediction in a multi-head CNN trained alongside class labels, a different method from training the standard network directly on random labels.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own random-label prediction results and regularizer comparisons. Figure 1B reports the learning-curve outcome in text; Figure 2 reports the common-regularizer comparisons graphically. It does not test shuffled pixels, Gaussian inputs, a sweep of corrupted-label fractions, or real-label-first learning dynamics.
record.test_reason: The study uses random-label predictability as a complexity metric. At λ = 0, the backbone learns class labels only; separately trained, class-conditioned heads predict random labels from its features. This does not measure standard networks trained on completely randomized targets or whether regularization prevents those networks from fitting them.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the main conclusion, but 'reduces memorization' should be qualified as reducing the proposed auxiliary-head metric. The authors acknowledge that memorization could move to earlier layers. They report no generalization improvement in the main experiment; appendices report conditional gains associated with learning-rate and label-smoothing effects, including a gain with augmentation at the optimal learning rate.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a multi-head CNN that predicts random labels alongside class labels; regularization is applied through an added random-label prediction objective. The random labels are not the sole training target.
record.method_sensitivity: Dropout probability, weight decay factor, and label smoothing factor change random-label prediction accuracy. Copy depth changes the reported accuracy in the separate VGG16 analysis; the authors state that accuracy rises between layers 5 and 7, within the convolutional part.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-layer, class-conditioned heads approach 100% random-label accuracy using features from a backbone trained on class labels. Their accuracy continues increasing after class-training accuracy approaches 100%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Class-trained representations retain sample-specific information sufficient for auxiliary random-label learning, whose learning curve can lag class prediction.

fits_no_version.finding: Dropout, weight decay, and label smoothing reduce random-label prediction accuracy at the probed representation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Common regularizers reduce random-label decodability by the tested auxiliary heads.

record.problems: The random-label results use added prediction heads and joint class-label training, limiting direct comparison to standard networks trained solely on random labels. The common-regularizer values are reported in figures without exact values in the text.

untested.parts: Direct fitting of completely randomized training targets by standard deep networks, with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters, and chance test performance.
Relative training time for true versus random targets and convergence across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training fit and test-error degradation across label-corruption fractions.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent direct random-label fitting; whether removing explicit regularization makes true-label generalization poor.

Signal-first learning followed by noise memorization in networks trained on noisy targets. Figure 1B compares class learning with separate auxiliary-head learning and does not establish this sequence within the claimed training process.

record.verdict_notes: The architecture difference alone is not a negative result against V1. Likewise, reduced auxiliary-head accuracy does not demonstrate that regularization prevents random-label fitting by the underlying network. Neither finding warrants the record's limits_scope verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test direct training of the standard network on a completely random labeling, test error at chance, or the original architecture and training setup; random labels are predicted by added heads while the feature network also learns class labels.

Measures common regularizers' effect on random-label prediction accuracy, but does not test whether removing them by itself makes generalization on true labels poor. It does not test data augmentation's effect on random-label fitting.

rows.subject: WideResNet-16-4
rows.operation_detail: Measured random-label prediction accuracy from added heads during joint class-label and random-label training.

conditions.value: SGD with momentum µ = 0.9; cosine learning rate scheduler; base learning rate η = 0.5; batch size 256; 200 epochs

rows.value: accuracy ... finally also reaches close to 100%
rows.note: The added random prediction heads share features with the class-label network; this is not direct training of the standard network on random labels.
rows.check: Near-100% accuracy is reported correctly, but belongs to auxiliary random-label heads whose loss does not train the backbone. The operation description incorrectly implies joint backbone training on class and random labels. This measures random-label decodability from class-trained features, rather than V1's training experiment.

rows.subject: WideResNet-16-4
rows.operation_detail: Applied dropout while evaluating random-label prediction accuracy.
rows.note: The authors state that dropout effectively reduces random-label accuracy; plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Dropout reduces auxiliary-head accuracy, but this does not establish whether a network trained directly on random labels can still fit them. Exact accuracies and condition-specific outcomes are unavailable in the supplied figure transcription; 'partial' is not established.

rows.subject: WideResNet-16-4
rows.operation_detail: Applied weight decay while evaluating random-label prediction accuracy.
rows.note: The authors state that weight decay effectively reduces random-label accuracy; plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Weight decay reduces auxiliary-head accuracy, but this does not establish whether a network trained directly on random labels can still fit them. Exact accuracies and condition-specific outcomes are unavailable in the supplied figure transcription; 'partial' is not established.

rows.subject: WideResNet-16-4
rows.operation_detail: Applied label smoothing while evaluating random-label prediction accuracy.
rows.note: The authors state that label smoothing effectively reduces random-label accuracy; plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Label smoothing is not one of V5's named regularizers. This experiment also measures auxiliary-head predictability rather than direct random-label fitting; reduced accuracy alone does not establish a partial claim effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: WideResNet-16-4 on CIFAR100 with added random-prediction heads and simultaneous class-label training
reader_labels.reason: Random-label training accuracy approaches 100%, but the experiment uses an added-head architecture and joint class-label training rather than the claim's original setup (R1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Dropout, weight decay, and label smoothing in the tested multi-head CIFAR100 setup
reader_labels.reason: Each regularizer reduces random-label prediction accuracy, qualifying the claim that these regularizers do not stop fitting; the paper does not report that they eliminate it (R2, R3, R4).
